name: When a market settles on one design
idea: An encyclopedia entry dates the idea of a dominant design to 1975. It defines one as the design that wins the market's allegiance, to which rivals must adhere to win a following. It states that the idea's originators saw its emergence as a milestone changing how firms compete. Later work, it states, argues that scale economies become important for competition only after such a design emerges.
suggests: Look at whether the products in a market now share a common set of key features, and if so whether rivals compete more on cost and scale than on new features.
limits: The entry notes that the 1975 work never uses the term dominant design. It states that a dominant design may not be better than other designs. Such designs, it adds, are often identified only after they emerge.
competing_idea: The entry states that two other works consider a disruption that enters a mature industry and starts a new cycle. In each cycle, it states, the number of firms rises, peaks with the dominant design and then falls.
questions: Have the products in this market settled on a common set of key features that buyers now expect?
Since then, has competition shifted toward cost and scale, and has the number of rivals fallen?
Is a new technology appearing that could start a fresh round of competing designs?

originals.reference: Wikipedia contributors, "Dominant design", Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia, revision 1296408217 of 19 June 2025
originals.about: James M. Utterback and William J. Abernathy, "A dynamic model of process and product innovation", Omega, Vol. 3 No. 6, December 1975, pp. 639-656
